items.item: Male and female incontinence sling placement
items.population: Patients with male or female pelvic anatomy
items.policy_summary: General Medicare coverage includes medically necessary surgery. This review did not establish code-specific nationwide sling coverage; a published RVU is not approval.
items.policy_scope: National general surgical benefit; individual coverage verification needed
items.disparity_evidence: July 2026 work RVUs: male 13.03, female 11.83. Physician facility total RVUs: 20.40 versus 19.87.
items.evidence_type: Published analogous pair plus direct CMS schedule extraction
items.limitations: Matched global periods do not prove equal operating time or total work. Not a causal bias estimate.
items.next_question: Which indication, prior treatments, procedure code and contractor apply?

items.item: Male and female sling revision or removal
items.indication: Clinically indicated correction/removal of an existing sling
items.policy_summary: General surgical coverage requires medical necessity. No universal code-specific approval was established; verify the complication, coding, setting and contractor.
items.policy_scope: National general surgical benefit; specific coverage unresolved
items.disparity_evidence: July 2026 work RVUs: male 13.15, female 10.87. Physician facility total RVUs: 21.45 versus 19.76.
items.evidence_type: Published analogous pair plus direct CMS schedule extraction
items.limitations: Comparability derives from the authors; equal global days alone do not establish equal resource use.
items.next_question: Is removal or revision necessary for a documented complication?

items.indication: Restore affected breast and contralateral symmetry
items.policy_summary: NCD 140.2 permits reconstruction of the affected and opposite breast after medically necessary mastectomy for any medical reason.
items.comparison: Implant-based versus autologous reconstruction; not male versus female
items.disparity_evidence: Two 2026 studies document unequal hourly valuation and declining inflation-adjusted breast-procedure payments.
items.evidence_type: National coverage plus empirical procedure-payment studies
items.limitations: Within-breast-procedure comparisons do not establish a patient-sex payment effect.
items.next_question: Which reconstruction method and setting are medically appropriate?

items.item: External breast prosthesis and postsurgical bra
items.policy_summary: Part B covers some external breast prostheses, including a postsurgical bra, after mastectomy. Supplier and item requirements apply.
items.comparison: External prosthesis versus surgically implanted reconstruction
items.disparity_evidence: No direct male/female Medicare denial or payment comparison identified for this item.
items.evidence_type: National coverage policy; disparity evidence gap
items.limitations: Coverage of some prostheses does not establish eligibility for every product or replacement frequency.
items.next_question: Does the ordered item meet supplier, documentation and replacement requirements?

items.item: Breast reconstruction solely for cosmetic reasons
items.indication: Appearance change without qualifying medical reconstruction
items.policy_summary: NCD 140.2 excludes reconstruction performed solely for cosmetic reasons.
items.comparison: Cosmetic purpose versus postmastectomy medical reconstruction
items.disparity_evidence: Purpose-based coverage distinction; not proof of a sex-based exclusion.
items.limitations: Do not apply this label to medically necessary postmastectomy reconstruction.
items.next_question: Is the documented purpose cosmetic or medically reconstructive?

items.indication: Persistent glandular enlargement causing significant symptoms
items.policy_summary: First Coast permits qualifying reconstructive surgery after specified evaluation/conservative treatment; cosmetic-only surgery and surgery as first-line treatment are excluded.
items.policy_scope: First Coast LCD L38914: Florida, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands; not nationwide
items.comparison: Symptomatic gynecomastia versus cosmetic chest contouring
items.disparity_evidence: Policy allows medically necessary male breast surgery; no matched denial-rate comparison identified.
items.limitations: Other jurisdictions may use different documentation criteria.
items.next_question: Are glandular disease, persistence, functional symptoms and prior treatment documented?

items.item: Reduction mammoplasty for symptomatic breast enlargement
items.indication: Functional symptoms attributable to enlarged breasts
items.population: Predominantly female patients; indication determines eligibility
items.policy_summary: First Coast distinguishes medically necessary reduction from appearance-only surgery; qualifying symptoms and local documentation requirements apply.
items.policy_scope: First Coast LCD L38914: Florida, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands; not nationwide
items.disparity_evidence: 2026 analysis found inflation-adjusted payments declined across all six studied breast procedures, including reduction.
items.evidence_type: Local coverage plus longitudinal Medicare fee analysis
items.limitations: Payment erosion within breast surgery does not prove sex discrimination; study lacks male comparator.
items.next_question: Does the applicable contractor find the functional indication adequately supported?

items.indication: Stress or urge urinary incontinence after unsuccessful exercise trial
items.population: Cognitively intact patients of any sex
items.policy_summary: NCD 30.1.1 covers practitioner-delivered biofeedback after four weeks of ordered pelvic exercises without significant improvement. First-line use remains contractor discretion.
items.comparison: Same national eligibility rule across sexes
items.disparity_evidence: No direct sex-specific Medicare coverage disparity established here.
items.limitations: This policy addresses incontinence, not every pelvic pain diagnosis or device.
items.next_question: Is a failed four-week exercise program documented?

items.policy_summary: NCD 30.1.1 explicitly excludes home biofeedback therapy.
items.disparity_evidence: Explicit setting-related exclusion affects both sexes.
items.limitations: Do not confuse biofeedback with covered nonimplantable pelvic electrical stimulation.
items.next_question: Is the requested product biofeedback or electrical stimulation?

items.indication: Refractory urgency incontinence, urgency-frequency or retention
items.policy_summary: NCD 230.18 covers test stimulation and qualifying implantation after failed conventional therapy. Permanent implantation requires at least 50% improvement. Stress incontinence and specified obstructive/neurologic conditions are excluded.
items.comparison: Eligibility depends on indication and trial response
items.disparity_evidence: No patient-sex payment or denial differential established in this review.
items.limitations: A diagnosis of incontinence alone does not qualify.
items.next_question: Does the indication and documented test response satisfy the NCD?

items.population: Cognitively intact patients of any sex
items.policy_summary: NCD 230.8 covers stimulation after four weeks of prescribed pelvic exercises fail to yield significant improvement.
items.comparison: Same eligibility rule; vaginal or anal delivery may differ
items.disparity_evidence: No direct sex-specific reimbursement differential established here.
items.limitations: This is not the same technology as home biofeedback.
items.next_question: Is the device correctly classified and the exercise trial documented?

items.item: Skilled pelvic-floor therapy for pain without incontinence
items.indication: Vulvodynia, nonspinal pelvic pain or other listed pelvic dysfunction
items.population: Patients with female or male pelvic conditions
items.policy_summary: Wellpoint A56566 lists specified non-incontinence pelvic dysfunction/pain interventions as noncovered skilled therapy; listed diagnoses also include prostatitis. Other jurisdictions must be checked.
items.policy_scope: Wellpoint J6/JK; current 04/01/2026 article; not a national exclusion
items.comparison: Local exclusion versus evidence of treatment benefit
items.disparity_evidence: Canadian RCT: 79% improved with multimodal PT versus 39% with lidocaine for provoked vestibulodynia.
items.evidence_type: Local restriction plus randomized clinical effectiveness evidence
items.limitations: RCT is not a Medicare payment study; not all older patients or pelvic conditions. Exclusion also lists male-associated disease.
items.next_question: Does current jurisdictional policy cover the specific diagnosis and intervention?

items.item: Surgical diagnosis or treatment of endometriosis
items.policy_summary: General surgery benefit may apply when medically necessary. This review did not verify a nationwide endometriosis-specific payment guarantee or exclusion.
items.policy_scope: National general surgical benefit; code/indication-specific coverage unresolved
items.comparison: Complex excision versus other gynecologic surgical work
items.disparity_evidence: Broader gynecologic valuation studies support further review; they do not establish an endometriosis-specific reimbursement effect.
items.evidence_type: Broader observational evidence; item-specific evidence gap
items.limitations: Do not infer noncoverage from missing dedicated disease codes or infer coverage from RVUs.
items.next_question: What exact operation, diagnosis, additional procedures and contractor rules apply?

items.item: Surgical repair of symptomatic pelvic-organ prolapse
items.policy_summary: Medically necessary surgery can fall under the general benefit. Procedure-specific nationwide approval was not established in this review.
items.policy_scope: National general surgical benefit; specific coverage verification needed
items.comparison: Different repair techniques; no inherently identical male comparator
items.disparity_evidence: Sex-specific surgical studies do not independently establish a prolapse-specific payment disadvantage.
items.limitations: Therapy exclusions for a prolapse diagnosis do not automatically exclude surgical repair.
items.next_question: Which repair, symptom severity, setting and contractor requirements apply?

studies.citation: Penn et al. Price and Prejudice: Reimbursement of Surgical Care on Male Versus Female Anatomies. J Womens Health. 2025;34:665–676.
studies.population: 55 analogous male/female procedure pairs; 110 CPT codes
studies.finding: Male procedures averaged 30% higher work RVUs, 25.6% higher physician facility-site payments and 20% higher nonfacility payments; 41/55 female procedures had lower RVUs.
studies.limitation: Selected anatomical pairs; no all-procedure estimate; excludes DRGs; limited operative-hour analysis; no causal identification.
studies.relevance: Direct patient-anatomy procedure valuation comparison; not clinician-gender pay.

studies.citation: Hathaway et al. Comparison of Work Relative Value Units Assigned to Urological and Gynecological Surgical Procedures. Urol Pract. 2024;11:654–660.
studies.design: Strictly matched procedure comparison using RUC methodology
studies.finding: Seven female procedures had higher work RVUs; three male procedures did. Overall differences in work RVUs and work RVUs per minute were not statistically significant.
studies.limitation: Small selected set; comparability criteria narrow scope. Nonsignificance does not prove equality across all services.
studies.relevance: Essential counterevidence; considered time, global periods, postoperative care and valuation dates.
studies.extraction_level: Abstract plus authors’ detailed AUA comparison table

studies.citation: Polan and Barber. Reimbursement for Female-Specific Compared With Male-Specific Procedures Over Time. Obstet Gynecol. 2021;138:878–883.
studies.payer: RVUs plus specialty compensation survey, not Medicare-paid dollars
studies.finding: Female procedures generated 10.6 versus 9.7 RVUs/hour, yet modeled specialty compensation was $555 versus $599/hour.
studies.limitation: Dollar estimates use employer/specialty compensation per RVU; do not call them different Medicare conversion factors. Perioperative work incompletely captured.
studies.relevance: Separates procedure value from specialty pay; not a direct clinician-gender effect.

studies.citation: Uppal et al. Discrepancies Created by Surgeon Self-Reported Operative Time and the Effects on Procedural Relative Value Units and Reimbursement. Obstet Gynecol. 2021;138:182–188.
studies.payer: NSQIP linked to CMS RVUs/time estimates
studies.finding: Median RVUs/hour: gynecology 10.2, orthopedics 14.3, neurosurgery 12.9. Differences persisted after clinical adjustment; reported-time excess correlated with RVUs/hour (r=.87).
studies.limitation: Specialty comparison, not isolated sex effect; registry and RUC time definitions/date comparability contested.
studies.relevance: Potential valuation mechanism; adjusted for age, comorbidities, stay length and predicted morbidity/mortality.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed

studies.citation: Goff et al. Is Adam worth more than Eve? The financial impact of gender bias in the federal reimbursement of gynecological procedures. Gynecol Oncol. 1997;64:372–377.
studies.finding: Male procedures paid more in 19/24 groups; reported average payment 44% higher and work RVUs 50% higher.
studies.limitation: Historical rates; judgment-based matching; not a present-day payment estimate.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed

studies.citation: Benoit et al. Comparison of 2015 Medicare relative value units for gender-specific procedures. Gynecol Oncol. 2017;144:336–342.
studies.payer: Medicare-related RVUs sourced from Department of Labor FECA data
studies.finding: Male procedures had higher work RVUs in 36/50 pairs; reported compensation was higher in 42/50 and averaged 27.67% higher.
studies.limitation: Global periods, postoperative care and valuation dates challenged by later authors; underlying FECA source limits simple Medicare interpretation.
studies.relevance: Historical valuation disparity; prioritize newer studies for current estimates.

studies.citation: Graziano et al. Longitudinal Trends in wRVU and Reimbursement for Free Flap and Implant-Based Breast Reconstruction: A 13-Year Valuation Analysis. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2026.
studies.design: Retrospective registry and longitudinal CMS valuation analysis
studies.finding: Implant reconstruction: median 1.4 hours and 11.94 wRVUs/hour; free flap: 6.77 hours and 6.29 wRVUs/hour. Free-flap hourly reimbursement improved but remained comparatively lower.
studies.limitation: Not all patients were Medicare beneficiaries; no male comparator; operating time does not capture all work.
studies.relevance: Within-women-care resource valuation; does not independently prove sex bias.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed

studies.citation: Stigliano et al. Trends in Medicare Reimbursement for Breast Procedures: A National and Geographic Analysis, 2010–2024. Ann Plast Surg. 2026;96:S228–S233.
studies.design: Longitudinal fee-schedule analysis and geographic comparison
studies.population: Six breast procedure types; 20 largest US cities
studies.finding: Inflation-adjusted payments declined 26.0%–46.2%; largest reduction involved tissue expanders. Geographic adjustments were much smaller than city cost-of-living differences.
studies.limitation: No male or nongynecologic control; fee schedules are not claims paid or proof of coverage.
studies.relevance: Evidence of erosion in breast-care reimbursement, not standalone proof of gender discrimination.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed

studies.citation: Doval et al. Is Our Effort Appropriately Valued? An Analysis of Work Relative Value Units in Immediate Breast Reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2020;146:502–508.
studies.population: 3,135 implant, pedicled-flap or free-flap reconstruction patients
studies.payer: Procedure RVUs and modeled dollars; mixed-payer registry
studies.data_period: Six-year period; dates not specified in abstract
studies.finding: Implant procedures yielded higher work RVUs and dollars per minute than flap reconstruction in all comparisons (p<.0001), despite shorter operative times.
studies.limitation: Operative time is incomplete workload measure; no male comparator; abstract does not fully specify reimbursement assumptions.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed

studies.citation: Morin et al. Multimodal physical therapy versus topical lidocaine for provoked vestibulodynia: a multicenter, randomized trial. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2021;224:189.e1–189.e12.
studies.population: 212 women recruited through four Canadian university hospitals/community
studies.payer: Clinical effectiveness study; not a reimbursement study
studies.finding: PT reduced intercourse pain more than lidocaine by 1.8 points; 79% versus 39% reported much/very much improvement. Benefits persisted at six months.
studies.limitation: Canadian, predominantly younger clinical population; no Medicare claim or sex comparison; cannot infer national coverage from efficacy.
studies.relevance: Relevant to reviewing pelvic-pain therapy restrictions against later clinical evidence.
studies.extraction_level: Citation and abstract; full-text extraction not completed
